title: Clark's Thinking with Demons: Intellectual History of Demonology
description: Stuart Clark published Thinking with Demons: The Idea of Witchcraft in Early Modern Europe in 1997, an 800-page intellectual history of demonological thought that fundamentally reoriented the field by taking demonological ideas seriously as theology and natural philosophy rather than treating them as irrational superstition to be explained away. Clark argued that demonology was a coherent, serious intellectual tradition that addressed real theoretical problems — about the nature of evil, divine providence, the limits of nature, and the basis of political authority — and that understanding witch prosecution requires engaging with this tradition on its own terms. His four-part structure (Science, History, Religion, Politics) showed how demonology was integrated into every domain of early modern learned culture.
historiographical_note: Clark's Thinking with Demons is a foundational text for the WitchcraftStudiesDB project's approach. His insistence that demonologists were 'thinking' — that their ideas had internal coherence and engaged real intellectual problems — is the basis of the Actor/Analyst distinction and the principle of 'rationality within framework' used in this database. The book's scale and ambition made it immediately controversial: it was criticized for neglecting social history and execution statistics in favor of ideas, while being celebrated for rehabilitating intellectual history of magic.
source_method: Clark, Thinking with Demons: The Idea of Witchcraft in Early Modern Europe (1997); subsequent scholarly responses
